'''Scott Sheffield''' is a professor of [[mathematics]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/ |title=Scott Sheffield |work= MIT.edu |accessdate=December 12, 2021}}</ref> His primary research field is theoretical probability.

==Research==
Much of Sheffield's work examines conformal invariant objects which arise in the study of two-dimensional statistical physics models. He studies the [[Schramm–Loewner evolution]] SLE(κ) and its relations to a variety of other random objects. For example, he proved that SLE describes the interface between two Liouville quantum gravity surfaces that have been [[conformal welding|conformally welded]] together.<ref>{{citation|arxiv=1012.4797 |last1=Sheffield |first1=Scott |title=Conformal weldings of random surfaces: SLE and the quantum gravity zipper |year=2010 }}</ref> In joint work with Oded Schramm, he showed that contour lines of the [[Gaussian free field]] are related to SLE(4).<ref>{{citation |arxiv=math/0605337|last1=Schramm|first1=Oded|last2=Sheffield|first2=Scott|title=Contour lines of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field|year=2006|bibcode=2006math......5337S}}</ref><ref>{{citation |arxiv=1008.2447 |last1=Schramm |first1=Oded |last2=Sheffield |first2=Scott |title=A contour line of the continuum Gaussian free field |year=2010 }}</ref> With [[Jason P. Miller|Jason Miller]], he developed the theory of Gaussian free field flow lines, which include SLE(κ) for all values of κ, as well as many variants of SLE.<ref>{{citation |arxiv=1201.1496 |last1=Miller |first1=Jason |last2=Sheffield |first2=Scott |title=Imaginary Geometry I: Interacting SLEs |year=2012 }}</ref>

Sheffield and Bertrand Duplantier proved the Knizhnik–Polyakov–Zamolodchikov (KPZ) relation for fractal scaling dimensions in Liouville quantum gravity.<ref>{{citation |arxiv=0808.1560 |last1=Duplantier |first1=Bertrand |last2=Sheffield |first2=Scott |title=Liouville Quantum Gravity and KPZ |year=2008 }}</ref> Sheffield also defined [[conformal loop ensemble]]s, which serve as scaling limits of the collections of all interfaces in various statistical physics models.<ref>{{citation |arxiv=math/0609167|last1=Sheffield|first1=Scott|title=Exploration trees and conformal loop ensembles|year=2006|bibcode=2006math......9167S}}</ref> In joint work with [[Wendelin Werner]], he described the conformal loop ensembles as the outer boundaries of clusters of Brownian loops.<ref>{{citation |arxiv=1006.2374 |last1=Sheffield |first1=Scott |last2=Werner |first2=Wendelin |title=Conformal Loop Ensembles: The Markovian characterization and the loop-soup construction |year=2010 }}</ref>

In addition to these contributions, Sheffield has also proved results regarding internal [[diffusion-limited aggregation]], [[domino tiling|dimers]], [[game theory]], [[partial differential equations]], and Lipschitz extension theory.<ref>{{Cite web | title=2011 Loève Prize announcement | url=https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/users/aldous/Research/sheffield.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205144549/https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/users/aldous/Research/sheffield.pdf | archive-date=2013-12-05}}</ref>

==Teaching==
Since 2011, Sheffield has taught 18.600 (formerly 18.440), the introductory probability course at MIT.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Teaching, Spring 2009 | url=https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/teach.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090814150734/http://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/teach.html | archive-date=August 14, 2009 | access-date=March 11, 2024 | url-status=live }}</ref>

Sheffield was a visiting professor at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] for the 2022 to 2023 academic year.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Scott Sheffield - Scholars {{!}} Institute for Advanced Study | url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/scott-sheffield | access-date=2025-01-03 | website=www.ias.edu}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Sheffield graduated from [[Harvard University]] in 1998 with an A.B. and A.M. in mathematics. In 2003, he received his Ph.D. in mathematics from [[Stanford University]]. Before becoming a professor at MIT, Sheffield held postdoctoral positions at [[Microsoft Research]], the [[University of California at Berkeley]], and the [[Institute for Advanced Study]]. He was also an associate professor at [[New York University]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://math.mit.edu/~sheffield/cv.html |title=CV |work=MIT |accessdate=August 23, 2013 }}</ref>

==Awards==
Scott Sheffield received the [[Loève Prize]], the [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers]], the [[Sloan Research Fellowship]], and the [[Rollo Davidson Prize]]. He was also an invited speaker at the 2010 meeting of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] and a plenary speaker in 2022. In 2017 he received the [[Clay Research Award]] jointly with [[Jason P. Miller|Jason Miller]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.claymath.org/events/news/2017-clay-research-awards |title=Clay Research Award 2017 |access-date=March 11, 2024 |archive-date=April 19, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230419202537/http://www.claymath.org/events/news/2017-clay-research-awards |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2021.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amacad.org/new-members-2021|title=New Members Elected in 2021|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=2021-04-22}}</ref> In 2023 he received the Leonard Eisenbud Prize for Mathematics and Physics of the [[American Mathematical Society|AMS]] jointly with [[Jason P. Miller|Jason Miller]]. In 2024, he received the [[Henri Poincaré Prize]] from the [[International Association of Mathematical Physics]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=ICMP 2024 |url=https://icmp2024.org/program-by-session.html |access-date=2024-07-14 |website=icmp2024.org}}</ref>
